html:
A declaration issued in November 2004 in Amman by King Abdullah II of Jordan, to state what Islam is and who counts as a Muslim, at a time when jihadist groups were killing other Muslims as unbelievers.

In 2005 the king called some 200 leading Islamic scholars from around 50 countries to Amman. They agreed on three points:

  • the eight main schools of Islamic law are all valid: the four schools of Sunni Islam, two of Shia Islam, the Ibadi school and the Zahiri school;
  • no one who follows these schools may be declared an apostate, a practice called takfir;
  • only qualified scholars may issue religious rulings, or fatwas.

Hundreds more scholars and institutions signed later, including al-Azhar and senior Shia clerics. It was one of the broadest agreements among Muslim scholars in modern times. It did not stop the sectarian violence of the Iraq war or the later rise of the Islamic State, but it gave mainstream clerics a shared text against them.
sum: A declaration issued in November 2004 in Amman by King Abdullah II of Jordan, to state what Islam is and who counts as a Muslim, at a time when jihadist groups were killing other Muslims as unbelievers.
